title: Poisson-burst adaptive warmup: throughput harness design notes
content:
Purpose and scope:

This note documents an alternative throughput harness approach we experimented with: a Poisson/Burst interarrival load generator combined with an adaptive warmup/priming phase. Goal is to get stable, repeatable throughput numbers while exercising realistic burstiness patterns and ensuring internal caches (KV, kernel caches, cuBLAS heuristics) and model memory paths are representative of production. This is not the final canonical protocol but captures observations, configuration recommendations, and acceptance criteria for repeatable bench runs.

Why a Poisson + burst model?
- Real traffic is rarely perfectly fixed-interval or completely uniform. Poisson arrivals more closely approximate user-driven API traffic for many product use cases, and explicit short bursts model microburst behavior from multiplexed frontends or sudden fan-out.
- Fixed-interval generators reduce one source of variability but can mask issues arising from queue build-up, scheduler jitter, and batching under bursty loads.

High-level methodology overview:
1) Pre-checks: assert cluster is healthy, GPU temperatures within normal, no competing jobs, node autoscaling disabled for run.
2) Baseline cold-run (optional): a small sample run from fully cold process to capture cold-start cost; keep separate from main throughput numbers.
3) Adaptive warmup/priming: ramp traffic using Poisson arrival + short bursts until a set of stability criteria are met (see details).
4) Measurement window: run stable load for a fixed measurement window, collect token-level telemetry, kernel-level traces on a small percentage of requests, and system-level metrics (GPU util, memory alloc patterns, PCIe counters).
5) Post-run checks and repeatability: repeat full run N times (default N=5) across different seed values; aggregate and check stability.

Load generator configuration recommendations:
- Arrival process: Poisson process defined by lambda (requests/sec). Implemented by sampling inter-arrival times from Exp(lambda) and scheduling requests accordingly. For burst modeling, overlay short burst events every T_burst seconds where for a period tb you increase lambda by factor B (e.g., 5x for 200ms).
- Request shape distributions: sample sequence lengths and context sizes from a recorded production distribution whenever possible. If synthetic, include 3 modes: short (<=64 tokens), medium (128–512), long (>=1024) with weights approximating workload.
- Payload templating: keep prompt and system message set deterministic per seed, but vary token-length via padding tokens so model path (attention length, KV cache size) is exercised. Avoid entirely random tokens — they produce different kv-caching behavior but also make output nondeterministic; use fixed pseudo-random sequences seeded per run.
- Concurrency targeting: configure generator to target an average concurrent requests value (lambda * avg_latency). Use closed-loop admission or open-loop depending on desired stress behavior. Document which was used.

Adaptive warmup (priming) algorithm:
Objective: reach a steady-state where throughput and latency metrics (mean, p95) have stabilized and internal caches have warmed.
- Start at a low lambda (10–20% of target).
- Every epoch (default 60s) increase lambda by a multiplicative factor (1.5x) up to target.
- In parallel, inject burst events (short, high-rate) every 30–90s to exercise batching and eviction behavior.
- After reaching target lambda, enter stabilization phase: run at target for at least M minutes (default 5m) and compute rolling statistics in sub-windows (30s). If the metric convergence criteria are met (see below), transition to measurement window. If not, continue additional stabilization epochs up to a max (default 20m).
- Convergence criteria (default):
  - Mean throughput deviation across last 4 sub-windows <= 2%
  - p95 latency deviation across last 4 sub-windows <= 5%
  - GPU effective utilization change <= 3% (optional; requires telemetry)
  - No sustained OOMs, kernel-launch failures, or internal retry storms

If convergence fails within max stabilization time, log diagnostic traces and abort run as "unstable".

Priming specifics to exercise internal runtime state:
- KV cache prefill: send a small set of long-context requests that purposefully fill KV cache with typical tokens (e.g., repeat templated preface). This helps ensure cache eviction behavior is realistic for long-context models.
- Kernel selection paths: for quantized models, run a few representative sequences that trigger different computational code paths (for different sequence lengths / attention patterns).
- cuBLAS/cuDNN warmup: run synthetic micro-benchmarks (short workloads) during warmup to self-prime GPU libraries' heuristics.

Measurement window and telemetry:
- Measurement window length: default 10 minutes after stabilization. Short tests (2–5m) are faster but will reduce statistical confidence.
- Sampling/tracing: capture full tracing (nvtx + runtime traces) for ~1% of requests, distributed across the window and bursts. Collect aggregated counters (tokens/sec, in-flight RPCs) at 1s resolution.
- Logs: persist per-request metadata (arrival timestamp, send timestamp, server start/end, latency, token counts, model version). Avoid logging full responses to keep storage small.

Repeatability protocol:
- Repeat the entire warmup + measurement run at least 5 times across different random seeds (affects Poisson RNG and payload seed). Seed list should be recorded.
- Acceptance for a benchmark configuration: across runs, median throughput difference <= 3% and p95 latency within +/- 5% across runs. If criteria fail, mark run as flaky and capture diffs in kernel traces.

Noise reduction and guardrails:
- Isolate the test nodes: ensure no other tenants, disable background backups, and pin CPU cores for loadgen process.
- Clock sync: ensure client and server clocks are NTP synced for correct latency attribution; prefer using server-side timestamps for most metrics.
- Network jitter control: run on isolated L2 or same subnet where possible. If benchmarking cross-AZ behavior is the goal, explicitly note increased variance.
- Randomization control: keep seeds recorded and rotate seeds deterministically across runs for reproducibility.

Edge cases and special scenarios:
- Cold-start measurement: keep a separate canonical cold-start benchmark where process restart and model load are part of the measurement. Use low sample counts but highlight 95th percentile cold setup time.
- Very long contexts: for models >4k context, extend warmup to allow longer KV cache evolution; consider priming with sequences that intentionally create eviction churn.
- Multi-model routing/fallback: if runtime includes automatic fallback to smaller variants, include explicit runs where fallbacks are disabled and others where enabled; compare throughput and failure modes.

Instrumentation suggestions for diagnosing instability:
- Request-level logs with NVTX spans and trace IDs to link host CPU timeline to GPU kernel activity.
- GPU metrics: SM utilization, achieved occupancy, memory throughput, L2 hit rate (if available), PCIe bandwidth.
- Scheduler/queue metrics: batch sizes over time, batch wait times, average KV-cache hits/misses by key size.
- Runtime internal counters: kernel selection path, quantization path taken, any upconversion path executed.

Example (human-readable) loadgen config snippet (describe, not nested JSON in this doc):
- mode: open-loop Poisson
- target_lambda: 120 req/s
- burst: every 45s, duration 250ms, multiplier 4x
- seq_length_distribution: [(short,0.6,32),(med,0.3,256),(long,0.1,1024)]
- warmup: adaptive (epoch=60s,multiplier=1.5,max_stabilize=20m,converge_windows=4)
- measurement_window: 10m
- repeat_runs: 5

Best practices and checklist before a benchmark run:
- [ ] Confirm cluster node health and no scheduled patches
- [ ] Collect baseline system footprint (running processes, GPU drivers)
- [ ] Record loadgen version and git commit
- [ ] Lock model version and rollout policy (no concurrent deploys)
- [ ] Export seed list and workload profile to artifacts store
- [ ] Enable NVTX tracing for 1% sample and system counters for entire window
- [ ] Run automated post-processing to compute acceptance metrics

Open questions / topics for follow-up experiments:
- How sensitive are convergence thresholds (2%/5%) to different model sizes? Should we use proportional criteria (e.g., absolute vs relative)?
- Evaluate closed-loop vs open-loop modes for latency-sensitive configs and whether closed-loop masks scheduler instability.
- Better heuristics for when kernel warmup (cuBLAS heuristics) materially affects numbers and whether we should standardize a library warmup microphase.

Notes and anecdotes from runs (short):
- On the 13B float16 variant we observed a 7% throughput drop when we omitted burst events in warmup; batcher never learned the high-short-latency path and kernel heuristic fell back to smaller kernels under load.
- A single jittery network link in AZ-2 added 30% variance to p95 in an otherwise stable run; lesson: document network topology in run metadata.

Summary:
Poisson-plus-burst arrival patterns with an adaptive warmup/priming phase produce more realistic and, importantly, diagnostic-friendly runs for throughput benchmarking. The cost is longer run times and slightly more complex orchestration, but the runs expose caching, kernel-selection, and scheduling phenomena that fixed-interval generators can hide. Adoption path: pilot this protocol for model onboarding runs and for any throughput benchmarks intended to represent customer-facing bursty traffic.

If you run this harness please push your run artifacts (seed list, kernel traces, aggregated metrics) to the linked GitHub loadgen run folder and file a lightweight report in the Confluence priming-playbook page.

-- Ava
